entries.title: Short on US Patriot missiles, Ukraine looks for alternatives
entries.summary: Russia is putting pressure on Ukraine with ballistic missiles, but Kyiv is short of Patriot interceptors. Domestic production and European alternatives take time. Can Kyiv realistically reduce its dependence on the US?
entries.content:
Ukraine

Short on US Patriot missiles, Ukraine looks for alternatives

August 12, 2026

Russia is putting pressure on Ukraine with ballistic missiles, but Kyiv is short of Patriot interceptors. Domestic production and European alternatives take time. Can Kyiv realistically reduce its dependence on the US?

Russia is increasingly relying on ballistic missiles for its attacks on Ukraine — precisely the weapons that Ukraine's armed forces depend heavily on Western support to ward off.

However, the crucial US-produced Patriot interceptor missiles are often in short supply.

How urgently does Ukraine need new Patriot missiles?

Extremely urgently. While Ukraine has set up a well-functioning defense network against drones, its armed forces are reaching their limits when it comes to fending off Iskander-M ballistic missiles. One of the few weapons capable of countering such missiles is, above all, the Patriot system with its PAC-3 interceptor missiles.

At the beginning of August, it became evident once again how patchy Ukraine's air defense has become. During a Russian attack on August 1, Ukraine could only intercept one of 27 ballistic missiles fired. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this was due to the fact that there were practically no more Patriot interceptor missiles left for the eight batteries stationed across Ukraine.

Three days later, according to Ukraine, Russia fired another 24 ballistic missiles as well as four Zircon hypersonic missiles, of which none were intercepted.

The French/Italian SAMP/T is considered an alternative to the Patriot system. However, Ukraine owns only a few of those, and the required Aster-30 interceptor missiles are also in short supply. In addition, the more powerful new-generation SAMP/T NG will only gradually become available. Therefore, the system is not a European short-term alternative to Patriot.

At the same time, Patriot deliveries are declining. According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine received only about one-third as many anti-aircraft missiles so far this year as it did in 2025. The war in the Middle East has further exacerbated the global shortage. Unlike at the beginning of the Ukraine war, the problem today lies less with launching facilities and more with Patriot ammunition.

What are the dimensions of Russia's missile capabilities?

Although exact Russian figures are not publicly available, there are numerous indications that Russia is ramping up its production. Moscow has, for example, significantly increased production of Iskander-M and Kinzhal ballistic and air-launched missiles. According to current estimates, it produces around 60 to 65 Iskander-M missiles per month alone, which amounts to more than 700 per year.

Reports indicate there are apparently shipments from North Korea as well. According to Ukraine, Pyongyang has supplied Russia with some 150 ballistic missiles since the end of 2023. In addition, a North Korean missile unit that has recently been deployed to Russia could be equipped with up to 120 additional missiles.

According to Ukraine's Defense Ministry, Russia launched 195 ballistic missiles of various types in July alone. Only 29 of them could be intercepted. Ukraine's military intelligence service estimates that Russia is currently capable of firing up to 100 ballistic missiles per month without depleting its stocks.

In contrast, US missile producer Lockheed Martin supplied only 620 modern PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles worldwide in 2025. The company plans to increase its annual production capacity to 2,000 units, but only as part of a seven-year program.

Did the US allow Ukraine to build its own Patriots?

According to defense intelligence platform Army Recognition, an average of only some 133 Patriot interceptor missiles have been delivered to Ukraine per year since the start of the war. Given the intensity of Russian missile attacks this isn't much, which is why another option is gaining importance in Kyiv: domestic production.

In the wake of the NATO summit in Ankara in July, the Ukrainian government presented the matter as largely settled. Zelenskyy cited a political decision by US President Donald Trump to grant Ukraine licenses for the production of Patriot interceptor missiles. As recently as July 28, it was declared after a meeting of the two leaders in Washington that both presidents had had talks about the "implementation" of this decision.

Three days later, Trump caused confusion. The US had not yet approved Ukrainian production; it had to be "careful," Trump said, with this kind of technology transfer.

Nonetheless, the talks are continuing. According to information from Reuters news agency, American and Ukrainian representatives are considering, among other options, a model in which components are produced in Ukraine and missiles are initially assembled in Germany. Kyiv's participation in the production of a new, less expensive Patriot missile is also under discussion.

How quickly could Ukraine build Patriot missiles on its own?

Not fast enough to solve the current problem of overburdening. Outgoing Ukrainian ambassador in Washington, Olha Stefanishyna, estimated that setting up production of Patriot missiles in Ukraine was a process that could take anywhere from 12 months to five years.

A modern interceptor missile has numerous highly specialized components. A shortage of seeker heads, electronics or missile motors, for example, can limit the entire production. Until a domestic production is established, Kyiv is trying to obtain Patriot missiles more quickly. To this end, other customers are to pass on their shipments to Ukraine and get replacements at a later date.

What's the status of Ukraine's own developments?

Ukraine is no longer working alone on a system of its own, but is trying to set up a European-Ukrainian missile defense project instead. The program is known as Freya.

The core of the system will be the FP7.X interceptor missile provided by Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point. According to the company's CTO, Iryna Terekh, its architecture is based on Soviet designs for the S-300 and S-400 air defense systems. Today's missile, however, had only some 20% in common with its predecessors, Terekh said.

Now involved in the project are, according to Fire Point, more than a dozen European arms manufacturers. Their goal is to develop an interceptor missile costing less than €1 million ($1.15 million), which would make it less expensive than the modern Patriot PAC-3 missiles ($5 million).

However, this system will not be quickly available either. The Ukrainian side aims to have a prototype ready during the first half of 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Europe braces for next heat wave
entries.summary: More than half the continent, including much of Germany, is set for a third wave of extreme heat this summer. The prolonged hot weather has significantly worsened wildfires and drought conditions across Europe.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

More than half the continent, including much of Germany, is set for a third wave of extreme heat this summer. The prolonged hot weather has significantly worsened wildfires and drought conditions across Europe.

Millions of people across Europe on Wednesday were set for more extreme heat, as yet another heat wave descends on the world's fastest-warming continent.

In France, Italy and Spain, some 92 million people are expected to swelter in temperatures exceeding 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) on Wednesday.

Some 300 million people — more than half Europe's population — will see temperatures pass 30 C.

The new heat wave comes after Western Europe saw its warmest ever June-July period, the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service(C3S) said on Monday.

According to C3S figures, temperatures in Europe are rising at twice the speed of other continents.

What temperatures are expected in Germany?

The German Weather Service has forecast highs on Wednesday of 34 C.

Temperatures are set to climb to 37 C on Thursday and as high as 39 C by Friday for much of western and southern Germany, the national meteorology agency said.

The looming heatwave is the third blast of extreme heat that Germany has seen this summer.

The prolonged heat has caused water levels on the Rhine to drop to record lows in some areas. The river is one of Europe's main waterways for transports of grain, minerals, fuel and other goods.

The drought conditions are impacting both Germany's environment as well as its economy, with companies that rely on goods normally transported via water suffering supply shortfalls.

France, Spain, Italy also brace for more heat

Extremely high temperatures of over 35 C are also forecast for France, Spain and Italy.

The latest blast of extreme heat comes just weeks after France and Spain faced some of the worst wildfires they have ever dealt with. 

In Spain, where several wildfires are still active, the national weather agency AEMET is warning of temperatures of over 35 C.

Millions of people are flocking to the Iberian country to watch the total solar eclipse on Wednesday.

Spanish authorities are deploying over 33,000 law enforcement personnel to eclipse observation areas and access points, many of which are suffering from drought conditions.

Officials are working to prevent these gatherings leading to more wildfires being started, urging visitors not to light any fires, litter or park their vehicles in areas with dry vegetation.

"High temperatures, the accumulated dryness of vegetation, and the intense pressure on natural areas due to projected travel necessitate extreme preventive measures," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said.

Heat wave set to extend from Balkans to UK

The heat wave is also set to spread to parts of southeastern Europe, including in Greece, Albania and Croatia.

Tens of millions of people in the United Kingdom are also bracing for temperatures to climb over 30 C. The UK's Met Office said Tuesday that the country is expected to record its hottest-ever summer this year.

Several European countries, including Germany, France and Spain, have all set new temperature records this summer.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Germany news: Cabinet approves intelligence service reforms
entries.summary: Germany's domestic and foreign intelligence services are to get greater powers to deal with hybrid threats. Meanwhile, transport ministers are meeting to find solutions to increasingly low river levels. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Cabinet approves intelligence service reforms

Published August 12, 2026last updated August 12, 2026

Germany's domestic and foreign intelligence services are to get greater powers to deal with hybrid threats. Meanwhile, transport ministers are meeting to find solutions to increasingly low river levels. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here's a roundup of the biggest stories hitting the headlines in Germany on Wednesday, August 12, 2026:

  • Cabinet approved reforms to the foreign and domestic intelligence agencies amid rising hybrid threats
  • Transport ministers are set to discuss possible measures as river cargo shipping is hampered by low water levels
  • The military reports a large increase in drone overflights of sensitive sites in recent years

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Interior minister hails 'new era' for Germany's secret services

Interior minister hails 'new era' for Germany's secret services

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has praised newly approved measures that give the country's intelligence services new, broad powers.

The reforms, which we reported on earlier in blog, will give Germany's domestic and foreign intelligence services more scope in gathering and storing information and data, as well as operational powers to fight acts of sabotage and hacking attempts.

The German government says the reforms are needed to allow the country to better combat the growing threat from cyber and hybrid attacks, particularly – but not exclusively — from Russia.

"We are transforming our intelligence services ​into genuine secret services," Dobrindt told a press conference in Berlin on Wednesday, adding that the new measures, which include artificial intelligence tools, will "revolutionize Germany's security architecture."

Germany's intelligence services were set up after the end of World War II, when memories of the Nazi regime were still recent, while people in the former East Germany lived under the oppression and intense state surveillance of the notorious secret state police, known as the Stasi.

Because of that legacy, Dobrindt said Germany was "catching up with what is possible in other European countries" such as France or the UK, whose secret services have more and broader powers.

Skip next section Rhine water level sinks further, stranding cargo vessels

Rhine water level sinks further, stranding cargo vessels

The water level in the Rhine River has fallen further amid the current heat wave, with German companies reporting increasing disruption to their supply and operations as cargo shipping is reduced or blocked.

The inland navigation agency WSV said the gauge at ​Kaub near Koblenz measured 12 cm (4.72 inches) on Wednesday, down from 15 cm on Tuesday.

It is well ​below the previous lowest recorded level of 25 cm in ​2018. ‌

The measurement indicates that the river at Kaub is now about 112 cm deep at its deepest point.

The low water at this chokepoint means that most vessels cannot pass through Kaub from either direction, effectively cutting the Rhine in two for commercial shipping.

Traders have told the Reuters news agency that sailings on northern sections of the river continue but are often only 20% full.

The Rhine is one of Europe's main arteries for transporting grains, fuels, minerals and manufactured goods.

Skip next section Rights group files criminal complaint over Mega's AI glasses

Rights group files criminal complaint over Mega's AI glasses

A German digital rights group, HateAid, has lodged a criminal complaint against Meta and companies that sell Meta's "smart" glasses in Germany.

HateAid said in a statement that putting the glasses — which can record audio and video — on the market broke digital privacy laws.

"There's no place to escape from smart glasses. You have to expect ​at ‌any moment to be filmed and then exposed on the Internet," said HateAid managing director Josephine Ballon.

The group said its complaint was based on a federal digital data protection law banning the sale of communication devices that can film people without their being aware of it.

Germany's digital communications ⁠regulator, ​the Federal Network Agency, issued a statement on smart ​glasses in late 2023, saying that connected devices for covert audio or video recordings were banned.

The glasses have earned the online sobriquet of "pervert glasses," with many fearing they could be used to take video particularly of unsuspecting women or children that is then turned into content of a sexual or hateful nature on the Internet.

Skip next section Inflation rises to 2.8% as energy prices jump

Inflation rises to 2.8% as energy prices jump

Germany's inflation rate rose to 2.8% in July, a rise caused mainly by an increase in energy prices after a fuel tax relief scheme expired, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) confirmed on Wednesday.

The figure is up 5 percentage points on the inflation rate in June.

"Energy prices continued to rise at an above-average rate and thus remained the central driver of inflation," said Destatis head Ruth Brand.

In July, consumers paid 8.3% more for fuel and heating than a year earlier, compared with an increase of just 3.4% in June.

In May and June, the government had cut energy taxes on petrol and diesel by just under €0.17 ($0.20) per liter as the US war with Iran drove oil prices up.

With the scheme expired, gasoline now costs more than €2 (2.31) a liter in most places.

The oil price shock was the key driver in pushing the April inflation rate to 2.9%, the highest since January 2024.

Food prices, for their part, have seen only moderate rises over the past months. In July, they were 0.4% above the same month a year earlier, matching the two preceding months.

Economists say, however, that food prices are likely to rise more sharply as the high energy prices make transport, refrigeration and storage are all currently more expensive.

Heat and drought are also negatively impacting agriculture and could reduce harvests.

Skip next section No accompanied drinking for 14-year-olds, Cabinet decides

No accompanied drinking for 14-year-olds, Cabinet decides

The German Cabinet also on Wednesday approved a draft bill abolishing a previous law allowing 14- and 15-year-olds to buy and drink beer, wine or sparkling wine when accompanied by their parents or guardians.

According to the bill, the current exception to the general ban on under 16-year-olds drinking any form of alcohol "weakens the protection of young people from the considerable health and social consequences of alcohol consumption."

In Germany, under 14-year-olds are currently not allowed to buy or drink alcohol in any form, while 14-15-year olds are permitted to purchase and drink undistilled alcohol in public places in the company of their parents or legal guardians.

From the age of 16, people are permitted to buy and consume undistilled alchohol without accompaniment, while those aged 18 and over, as legal adults, can buy and consume all alcoholic beverages.

Skip next section Cabinet approves child pension subsidy

Cabinet approves child pension subsidy

Among the draft bills approved by the Cabinet on Wednesday is a plan for children from the age of 6 to receive €10 ($11.54) from the state every month for a pension deposit .

Under the plan, the child's parents or carers would open the account and be able to deposit money there themselves as well.

The state payments would continue until the child turns 18.

Pension payments from the account would flow only after the now-adult turns 65.

According to the Finance Ministry, the state subsidies would amount to around €2,200, which "could become around €53,000 by pensionable age without any additional payments."

With the plan, the government aims not only to guarantee better financial security in old age for the younger generation but also to educate it in financial matters.

"Someone who experiences the capital market already at a young age and has positive experiences with it develops an understanding of long-term investment and will tend to invest in the capital market during his or her life," the Finance Ministry said.

The bill still needs approval by both chambers of parliament to go into force.

Skip next section Cabinet passes controversial intelligence agency reform

Cabinet passes controversial intelligence agency reform

The German Cabinet has approved a more than 700-page package of laws granting much greater powers to both the domestic intelligence agency (BfV) and the foreign intelligence agency (BND).

The package will allow the agencies more latitude in the gathering and storage of information and data, along with new options to actively combat acts of sabotage and hacking attacks.

The government says the package aims to enable the agencies to operate more effectively in the face of a myriad of hybrid security threats.

"We will not look on passively as foreign interference, sabotage and threats to the pillars of our constitution and our free society continue to grow," chancellery head Nina Warken told the daily Rheinische Post.

"Our [intelligence] services can only take targeted action against these hybrid attacks if they have more liberties and up-to-date measures" at their disposal, she said.

However, the planned reform has also met with considerable criticism from those who see the extended powers as a threat to civil rights.

The leader of the Free Democrats (FDP), Wolfgang Kubicki, accused Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of "breaking a taboo."

"It can hardly be imagined that the Constitutional Court will not intervene here," he told the Augsburger Allgemeine daily. 

"I do not want any secret police in Germany," he said. "I want full court control in the case of attacks on basic rights and a state that understands that you don't defend liberty by curbing it."

Skip next section Ansah has 'no fear' of losing bronze despite looming doping ban

Ansah has 'no fear' of losing bronze despite looming doping ban

Sprinter Owen Ansah, Germany's 100-meter record holder, delivered his country's first men's 100-meter European Championship medal in 40 years, despite facing a potential doping suspension.

Ansah won the bronze at the European Championships in Birmingham, England on Tuesday night, to take the biggest win of his career.

The 25-year-old posted a time of 10.19 seconds, managing to shut out the considerable noise surrounding his looming suspension by Germany's National Anti Doping Agency (NADA), which accuses the sprinter of refusing to take a doping test on July 9.

But Ansah insists that he failed to provide a urine sample because the doping control officer arrived outside of the requested time slot and Ansah had to leave to travel to Monaco for a Diamond League event. He also says he had just used the restroom before the officer arrived.

He said he is "not afraid" of having his medal revoked. "I trust my team, which has my back. I can’t influence the other stuff. I can only influence how fast I am on the track. And I showed that well today," Ansah said.

The sprinter is now turning his attention to the 200-meter dash on Friday, where he is eyeing a second medal at the Championships.

Skip next section Drone-related security incidents on the increase — military

Drone-related security incidents on the increase — military

Several hundred security incidents involvingdrones have been registered by Germany's armed forces in the past years, a military spokesman has said.

"Since the start of the illegal full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, reports on drone sightings affecting the Bundeswehr have greatly increased," the spokesman told the media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland.

"Over the past few years, several hundred suspected drone overflights in Bundeswehr-related areas have been reported," he said, adding that whole swarms of drones had been sighted on occasion.

Germany has seen a number of drone incidents in recent weeks, including one involving a drone carrying explosives at the Leipzig-Halle airport.

According to the newsmagazine Spiegel, the Hannover-Langenhagen airport was also closed several times overnight to Tuesday after a drone was sighted by employees.

Spiegel reported that the drone did not show up on police detection devices, suggesting that the object was possibly not a commercially available model.

Skip next section Transport ministers to meet over low river levels

Transport ministers to meet over low river levels

Transport ministers from Germany's state and federal governments are to hold a video conference on Wednesday to discuss the challenges to inland shipping as rivers across the country run low.

Federal Transport Minister Steffen Bilger said the ministers would, among other things, talk about ways to compensate potential supply shortages as ships transport less cargo.

Several states have already lifted a ban on trucks using highways on Sundays in a bid to shift some cargo transport to other routes.

Ahead of the conference, Bilger, who belongs to the center-right Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, told the daily Rheinische Post that there were currently no supply shortfalls.

However, he also said that cargo transport needed to be shifted more to road and rail to reduce the risk of supply problems to industry.

Bilger said the current river water shortages would likely continue until the end of August at least.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

DW's newsroom in Bonn wishes all its readers guten Tag on what promises to be another very warm summer day.

Amid the hot and dry weather, water levels in rivers such as the Rhine are continuing to drop, causing problems to inland shipping and to companies that rely on it for their supplies.

The situation on Germany's waterways will thus be a main topic in today's blog once again, as transport ministers meet to discuss how best to remedy the situation.

A planned reform granting new powers to intelligence agencies is also causing a stir, with some saying they go too far while others maintain their necessity as Germany faces ever more hybrid security threats.

One of those threats has been highlighted in a military report saying that hundreds of drone flights over army sites have been sighted in the past few years.

Read on for more on these and other stories hitting the headlines in Germany.

entries.title: EU packaging rules: Why small firms are sounding the alarm
entries.summary: The EU has introduced new rules targeting packaging waste and "forever chemicals." Although the changes will be phased in slowly, some small sellers have already paused shipments due to the additional red tape.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

The EU has introduced new rules targeting packaging waste and "forever chemicals." Although the changes will be phased in slowly, some small sellers have already paused shipments due to the additional red tape.

What changes from Wednesday?

In a drive to cut waste and improve public health, new European Union rules take effect on Wednesday, banning high levels of PFAS "forever chemicals" in packaging.

Under the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), any new packaging products entering the market will now have to meet tighter standards if designed to come into contact with food.

PFAS have been linked to increased risks of certain cancers and other health conditions. 

Although the amount of material people are exposed to from food packaging is usually low, scientists are worried about the long-term effects.

After all, PFAS are highly persistent chemicals and accumulate in the body and the environment.

PFAS are used to make paper and cardboard packaging both grease- and water-resistant and are found in everything from pizza boxes to TV dinners.

Packaging with lower PFAS reduces the risk of these persistent chemicals migrating into food or the natural world when thrown away.

The new rules are in addition to curbs on bisphenol A (BPA) in food-contact materials, which took effect across the EU last month.

Under PPWR, businesses will not be required to recall or destroy packaging or goods that were already on the market before Wednesday.

While consumers won't notice any difference, businesses have fiercely criticized the changes, which also require packaging to meet new sustainability standards.

Are the new packaging rules too complicated?

Many small businesses and online traders believe the additional cost and red tape are too cumbersome.

They complain that they now have to register their packaging in multiple EU states, often with fees.

"Instead of facilitating cross-border trade, the new rules threaten to make it significantly more difficult," warned Händlerbund, the German online retailers' association.

Händlerbund warned its members: "There is no minimum quantity and no exception for small businesses."

EU lawmaker Elisabeth Dieringer of the far-right Freedom Party of Austria has warned that PPWR would mean five-figure costs for medium-sized firms.

"While corporations have their own departments for this [red tape], the Mittelstand [medium-sized firms] has little choice but to 'eat or die,'" she wrote on X on Tuesday.

Several businesses, from sole traders to medium-sized firms, said they had paused deliveries to and within the EU due to the new rules.

"Under these rules, I would need to appoint an authorized representative in every single EU country I send to," wrote the owner of a small online store, Monstaas Workshop, in an Instagram post.

"The cost is around €300 ($346) per country, per year ... these costs are simply not affordable."

Swedish embedded electronic devices maker iLabs Electronics said it would halt web shop orders from EU countries.

"The cost and administrative burden [of PPWR] is now out of proportion to our direct sales volume," iLabs wrote on its website.

A petition on change.org had been signed by more than 45,000 people by Wednesday morning, calling on Brussels to "stop destroying EU micro-businesses."

How bad is the EU's packaging waste problem?

According to the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm, EU countries have witnessed a 20% increase in packaging waste over the last decade.

Without PPWR, Brussels says, discarded packaging was set to rise by another 19% by 2030, driven by the boom in online shopping and convenience food.

EU data shows that 178 kilograms (392 pounds) of packaging waste was generated per person across the bloc in 2023. Of this, 35.3 kg was plastic packaging, only 42% of which was recycled.

At 215 kg per capita (in 2023), Germany's waste from packaging is much higher than the EU average.

Each EU resident generates the equivalent of roughly half a kilo of packaging waste every day, data from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency, shows.

According to Brussels, the volume of waste has grown faster than recycling rates over the past decade.

Packaging also ⁠accounts ⁠for about 40% of plastic consumption in Europe, an EU official told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday.

What are the EU's long-term waste targets?

Although PFAS is the main focus of this initial phase of PPWR, the EU has set binding targets to cut packaging waste by 5% by 2030 and 15% by 2040.

From 2028, packaging manufacturers will be required to carry standardized labels that clearly show the materials used and how it should be recycled or disposed of.

Some stores, particularly restaurants and cafes, will be required to offer customers reusable packaging as an option, often at no extra charge.

Deposit-and-return schemes for plastic bottles and soda cans, such as those operational in Germany and the Netherlands, will be rolled out across the EU by 2029.

Then from 2030, all packaging placed on the EU market, including single-use plastic bottles, must be designed to be recyclable.

Packaging will also be required to be kept to a minimum to protect the product and fulfill its function.

This measure is meant to reduce the overuse of packaging for marketing purposes.

Meanwhile, single-use plastic packaging for fresh produce will be banned from 2030.

EU states will be able to set their own penalties for non-compliance, with German authorities allowed to impose fines of up to €200,000 ($230,000) for more serious breaches.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

entries.title: AI helping create popular mobile sports games
entries.summary: After the World Cup and before the domestic season, many fans still crave more football. Amateur coders are helping to fill this gap.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

AI helping create popular mobile sports games

August 12, 2026

After the World Cup and before the domestic season, many fans still crave more football. Amateur coders are helping to fill this gap.

After the World Cup and before the domestic football season begins, the world's most popular sport tends to enjoy a relatively quiet period. For some though, the need for football remains.

This summer that demand has been met by the creation of a raft of mobile sports games in which players can dive into nostalgia and storytelling. This craze has seemingly been inspired by the viral 82-0 basketball game in which players can draft an all-time NBA starting five by spinning a random wheel for teams and decades.

Inspired by this, Deniz Sancar, a hobbyist coder who works in advertising, created 38-0-0. Sancar told Mobilegamer.biz that despite having no previous coding experience, he built the game overnight with Claude Code, an advanced AI assistant that is designed to help with coding. The game was No. 1 in the UK App Store games charts in June.

Destiny Eleven: From TikTok to France and the world

Another example is Destiny Eleven. Maxence Pigne, a PSG fan and a project manager, was inspired by a game he saw on TikTok that allowed players to play out the career of a professional footballer. After the 2026 World Cup, Pigne released his version, also created with the help of AI assistant Claude, which took the original idea further by offering more variety and choices in the career.

The man who specializes in computer science told French weekly Le Point that the decision to publish the free game earlier than planned paid off because by the end of July, the game had over 1 million players with 14 million careers having been created. Leverkusen striker Martin Terrier is reportedly a fan of the game, which has seen many variations in different languages emerge in the weeks since its arrival.

Mobile games are big business

It's clear mobile games have come a long way since Nokia released "Snake" back in 1997. They are now big business. According to digital market intelligence platform Sensor Tower, approximately 50 billion mobile games were downloaded in 2025, generating $82 billion (€71 billion) in in-app purchases. According to Game, the German games industry association, revenue in Germany in 2025 was approximately $3.12 billion, with 28.1 million players.

"This clearly indicates that mobile gaming in Germany is no longer a niche topic, but rather a serious genre with significant purchasing power," Kyle Kuscu, chairman of the German Mobile Gaming Association, told DW. 

"This is also relevant for the esports sector: Germany has a broad player base, and mobile gaming is the largest platform in the country in terms of user numbers."

This summer, the emergence of sports-drafting games has clearly benefited from a World Cup summer but also because of game design.

"The World Cup or tournament effect only amplifies this, but it doesn't fully explain the hype on its own," Kuscu said.

"Such games satisfy a fundamental human need shared by many users: control, optimization and imagination in a very compact format — in other words, the feeling of having it all in your own hands, of building the perfect team or career, without a long learning curve or complex controls."

What counts is the 'idea and final execution'

AI has been involved in video game creation for years, but with smarter and faster AI in 2026 comes an even more financially efficient approach for game developers. This is particularly important in the tough economic conditions in which free-to-play mobile games operate.

"The trend toward smaller, faster-to-develop games with AI support is likely to continue and may even grow. But I don't believe that every viral success story will be repeated," Kuscu said.

"Based on our own experience and confirmed by external sources, we know that AI has long been used extensively and intensively in game development, especially for coding, prototyping, research and repetitive tasks. At the same time, many people remain skeptical about quality, dependencies and creative limitations. Even if we advocate for the use of AI-assisted programming, what ultimately counts is the idea and the final execution of a game, and that won't change."

Short shelf life a key problem in a competitive market

The challenges for such games to maintain their success remains a major challenge though, especially given the overall gaming market remains a far from profitable industry. More teams can release more games, but that makes competition stiffer than ever.

"The biggest hurdle is no longer just production, but the business model behind it: Mobile games are extremely dependent on user attention, repeat usage, and, above all, in-app purchases," Kuscu said.

"A viral launch does not yet equate to a viable, let alone successful, business. They must get a handle on session duration, community building, update frequency and monetization very quickly. This is precisely where the crux of the matter lies, because otherwise the hype will fizzle out before the game can become a sustainable title."

Whether it's the immersive storytelling nature of these games or the ease with which a virtual world can be reached, it's clear that these games have found a gap in the market. History suggests they might not be popular for long, but even if this summer is their moment in the sun, their emergence appears a significant reminder of the challenges the mobile game industry will face with the increased involvement of AI.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Zambia's 2026 election: Key issues to watch
entries.summary: Economic recovery, youth turnout, women's representation and judicial independence are among the issues shaping Zambia's vote on Thursday.
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambia's 2026 election: Key issues to watch

August 12, 2026

Economic recovery, youth turnout, women's representation and judicial independence are among the issues shaping Zambia's vote on Thursday.

Zambia's general election on Thursday will be fought on economic recovery, governance reforms and a sweeping change to the country's parliamentary map.

Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND), is seeking a second term against 14 opponents.

His principal challenger is Brian Mundubile, a former ally of the late President Edgar Lungu, who has surged to the front of a fragmented opposition after being backed by a coalition of rival parties.

The Electoral Commission announced in April that 70 new constituencies would be added, raising the number of parliamentary seats from 156 to 226, creating smaller, more local voting districts. Up to 8.7 million voters are expected to take part in the elections, a majority of whom are women.

Economic issues dominate Zambia's election campaign

Economic issues dominate voters' concerns. Official data shows that over 70% of the population lives on less than three dollars a day, and many households survive on salaries between $60 and $100 (€52 and €87) a month while grocery prices keep rising.

"I would like the new government to increase our salaries. [Maize meal] is very expensive. Everything is expensive," said security guard Lucky Mutelo.

Rebecca, a market shopper, echoes the sentiment, noting that "the cost of living is still too high."

The government has been making significant gains on these issues.

Hichilema's government has secured a landmark debt restructuring agreement, restoring an International Monetary Fund program and supporting economic growth. Inflation fell to 6.5% in June this year.

The administration has also rolled out free education and an expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.

Nevertheless, a historic drought that crippled agriculture and forced severe hydro‑power load‑shedding has strained household finances.

Election demographics amid a fragmented electoral field

To become president, a candidate must secure 50% plus one of the total votes cast. If no contender reaches this threshold, the two highest‑scoring candidates will face off in a second round — a mechanism designed to ensure that the president enjoys a clear popular mandate.

There are 14 names on the ballot, so even small swings in support across the 10 provinces could determine whether the election goes to a second round.

Analysts say the election's outcome would hinge on urban centers such as Lusaka and the Copperbelt, where cost‑of‑living pressures are most acute, while rural provinces traditionally follow established party loyalties.

Rural voters in the Southern, Western and North‑Western provinces historically back the UPND, whereas the opposition targets the Northern, Luapula and Eastern provinces.

Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported that the high youth turnout that propelled the current president Hakainde Hichilema to a landslide victory in 2021 is expected to be a decisive factor again, especially in densely populated urban districts.

Nearly half of registered voters are aged between 18 and 35, making young people a potentially pivotal bloc, Institute for Security Studies researcher Zenge Simakoloyi told AFP.

Can women swing Zambia's election?

Gender representation is another prominent theme. In this election, there is one female presidential candidate and four female running mates.

Mwaka Nyirenda is one of a handful of women contesting for a parliamentary seat.

"Politics is still a man's world. People doubt you, underestimate you and try to intimidate you," she told DW, noting that the financial bias still favors male candidates.

Women comprise roughly 51% of Zambia's population but hold only about 15% of parliamentary seats, and fewer than 20% of political leadership positions.

Leah Diana Mitaba, publicity secretary of the Non‑Governmental Coordinating Council, warns that these figures "demonstrate that Zambia remains far from achieving the 50:50 gender representation envisaged in the Constitution, the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development, the African Union Agenda 2063 and the UN Sustainable Development Goals."

Girls Gone Political, a civil‑society group, campaigns for greater female participation. Its leader, Dorothy Mtanga, thinks more civic education is needed. "There's the need for sustained democratic civic education to ensure that more women are elected into office," she said.

Judicial independence called into question

This election also raises questions about the independence of Zambia's judiciary.

In 2024, President Hichilema suspended three Constitutional Court judges who ruled in favor of his rival, former President Edgar Lungu.

Lawyer Linda Kasonde argued that "judicial independence is the ability to adjudicate on any matter, without fear or favor, regardless of the stakes involved in the case." In practice, opposition lawyers think the executive is trying to interfere with justice delivery.

Kasonde identifies two recent concerns. First, an executive‑approved salary increase for judges that bypassed the constitutional emoluments commission.

"The government increased salaries for judicial officers in 2025 outside the proper procedure, raising questions about whether the process was independent," she told DW.

Second, the appointment of 16 new judges in early 2026, many of whom hail from the incumbent's strongholds.

"These appointments call into question whether any decisions that will be made regarding the elections will be done independently," lawyer Kasonde concluded.

Amnesty International says Zambian laws, including the Public Order Act and cybercrime legislation, have been weaponized to restrict dissent, opposition gatherings and freedom of expression. It also warns that the increasing use of criminal charges against government critics could have a chilling effect on political expression.

Chief Justice Mumba Malila recently reassured the public.

"The judiciary stands ready to discharge its constitutional responsibility, independently, professionally and within the strict timelines established by the law," he said. Critics, however, maintain that true independence requires full structural and financial autonomy from the executive.

Continuity or change in Zambia?

Zambia's status as one of the region's stable multi‑party democracies in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) means that this election will influence regional democratic norms.

The country's ability to host a peaceful transition or renewal of power is a barometer for neighboring states, especially after recent defeats of incumbents in Botswana and Malawi.

Polls will be open from 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Zambians will elect a president, National Assembly members, mayors, councilors, and council chairs.

This election holds the potential to either consolidate President Hichilema's reform agenda or usher in a new administration.

This article was compiled from several DW video reports covering Zambia's 2026 general election.

entries.title: Solar eclipse: What to look forward to
entries.summary: The last solar eclipse visible from the European mainland was in 1999. Here's what to expect, and how to prepare for this rare occasion.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

The last solar eclipse visible from the European mainland was in 1999. Here's what to expect, and how to prepare for this rare occasion.

On Wednesday, about 980 million people across parts of the Northern Hemisphere will have the chance to observe this upcoming solar eclipse.

They will be joined by hosts of researchers who will be taking advantage of the fleeting minutes when the sun's corona is visible from Earth to test specialized instruments and capture rare images. With them, they hope to gain a deeper appreciation of the material above the sun's surface.

What's going to happen?

During a solar eclipse, the moon orbits between Earth and the sun during the daytime, casting a shadow which temporarily darkens the sky and appears to blot out the sun. At the height of an eclipse, the moon's disk appears to align with the sun, revealing the sun's corona — its outermost atmosphere that flares outward like a crown (hence the name).

As the moon approaches and the sky darkens, you might also notice the temperature dropping, shadows appearing crescent-shaped, the wind beginning to shift and animals behaving unusually.

Solar panels will be able to produce less energy in this time. In Germany, this is expected to lead to a brief surge in electricity prices.

Right before the eclipse reaches its maximum point, known as totality, watch out for Baily's beads. These are the final rays of sun reaching Earth through valleys on the moon's surface. They appear as white specks encircling the moon like a string of pearls.

As night closes in during totality, keep an eye out for the stars that appear. Some might even be able to catch a glimpse of auroras or passing meteors.

Where will the eclipse occur?

If you live in Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, northern Spain or northeastern Portugal, you're in luck! Viewers in these locations will be able to observe a total solar eclipse.

In most of Western Europe, as well as parts of northern Africa and northern America, astronomy enthusiasts will still be able to watch a partial solar eclipse.

And this is just the first of two eclipses in August. The second will take place on August 27-28, when Earth moves between the sun and the moon to create a lunar eclipse.

The next solar eclipse will happen February 2, 2027, over much of Africa, South America, as well as parts of Antarctica.

While eclipses themselves are fairly frequent occurrences, it's not that often that a total solar eclipse is visible on inhabited parts of the globe. The last solar eclipse visible for most of mainland Europe, for example, was in 1999.

What time is the eclipse happening?

The spectacle will begin at 15:34 GMT, with the moon slowly dimming the sun's light as it creeps into position. About two hours later, at 17:46 GMT, the eclipse will reach totality for about two minutes.

But where on the globe you are watching from will make a difference. While Icelanders will be able to observe the eclipse's totality at 17:48 GMT, viewers in Spain will have to wait until 18:27 for their chance.

Where can I watch the eclipse?

Since the eclipse is happening relatively late in the day, viewers are recommended to watch from high places to catch a good view of the sun as it dips toward the horizon. Most west-facing hills, towers and (safe) rooftops with an unobstructed view should do the trick.

If you're the kind who prefers crisper images, NASA is also offering a livestream.

Can I wear normal sunglasses to watch the eclipse?

In short, no. Looking directly into the sun can cause permanent damage to the retina at the back of your eye. Ordinary sunglasses, even polarized ones, are far too weak to provide enough protection.

Instead, you'll need certified ISO 12312-2 glasses, available at most pharmacies and opticians. Most are sold out already, but there are plenty of directions online for building a pinhole camera to safely watch the eclipse with small children.

You can also use a kitchen colander, or any other tool with small holes, to project tiny crescent-shaped shadows onto a safe surface.

Whether or not you are wearing eclipse glasses, never look at the sun through a camera, telescope or binoculars without a specialized filter, as the concentrated light can cause serious damage to your eyes.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler

entries.title: India news: IndiGo engine failure triggers airport emergency
entries.summary: Chennai airport declared full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, hours after reports that an Air India pilot involved in an on-air incident last week tested positive in a drug test. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: IndiGo engine failure triggers airport emergency

Published August 12, 2026last updated August 12, 2026

Chennai airport declared full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, hours after reports that an Air India pilot involved in an on-air incident last week tested positive in a drug test. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, August 12:

  • Chennai airport declared a full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure
  • The pilot of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week tested positive for marijuana
  • Food safety, hygiene issues plague India's quick commerce firms
  • Supreme Court urges faster adjudication of West Bengal SIR appeals
  • Seven killed, more feared trapped after landslide in Mumbai
  • Parliamentary panel finds charges proved against judge over burnt cash found at home

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Tata Sons' chairman will not seek reappointment at end of term

Tata Sons' chairman will not seek reappointment at end of term

Indian conglomerate Tata Sons' Chairman N Chandrasekaran said on Wednesday he would not seek reappointment when his term ends in February.

The 63-year-old, who has led Tata Sons since 2017, cited a lack of board support amid tensions with the charity arm, Tata Trusts, which controls 66% of the conglomerate's holding company.

Chandrasekaran said uncertainty over the leadership situation had remained unresolved for six months and that a decision was important for employees, investors and other stakeholders.

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata opposed Chandrasekaran's reappointment at a February board meeting, Reuters reported.

Skip next section Seven killed, more feared trapped after landslide in Mumbai

Seven killed, more feared trapped after landslide in Mumbai

At least seven people were killed and several injured after a landslide hit Mumbai's Kurla area early Wednesday following heavy rain, the Hindustan Times reported.

According to the report, the landslide occurred around 3 a.m. local time, with more people feared trapped, Deputy Commissioner of Police Ganesh Shinde said.

Rescue operations are underway, with teams from various emergency agencies deployed.

Mumbai has experienced heavy monsoon rain in recent weeks, causing waterlogging and disruptions to air and road traffic.

Skip next section Two people killed in Mumbai fire

Two people killed in Mumbai fire

Two people, including a two-and-a-half-year-old, were killed and eight others injured after a fire broke out in two apartments on the 11th floor of a residential building in Mumbai late Tuesday, officials said.

The fire broke out around 10 pm in Vile Parle West area and was brought under control shortly after midnight on Wednesday.

Skip next section Supreme Court urges faster adjudication of West Bengal SIR appeals

Supreme Court urges faster adjudication of West Bengal SIR appeals

India's Supreme Court on Tuesday urged tribunals handling appeals against voter deletions in West Bengal to speed up their work, saying the process could not drag on indefinitely, a report in the Times of India said.

Nearly 3.4 million appeals are pending before tribunals set up to hear challenges to deletions from electoral rolls during a Special Intensive Revision (SIR), according to the court.

"The process cannot be so slow that the next assembly elections would be due by the time the appeals are decided," Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said, according to the report.

India's election commission conducted the SIR of electoral rolls in several states and territories ahead of state election, including West Bengal, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party recently won state elections.

The commission said the "intensive revision" was needed to remove the names of deceased individuals, those who have permanently moved and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."

Critics of the SIR say it is skewed against marginalized and minority communities.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Disrupted monsoons force India to face climate threat

IN DEPTH: Disrupted monsoons force India to face climate threat

For generations, India has lived by the rhythm of the southwest monsoon. But with the country hit by dry spells, cloudbursts and deadly floods, climate swings now expose the costs of building for yesterday's weather.

Skip next section Food safety, hygiene issues plague India's quick commerce firms

Food safety, hygiene issues plague India's quick commerce firms

India's quick commerce sector, especially grocery delivery services, is in the doldrums as authorities flag serious food safety and hygiene violations.

Authorities in the southern Karnataka and western Maharashtra states sealed a Zepto warehouse on Tuesday and suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after inspections found serious violations, reports said.

In Karnataka, a Zepto warehouse near Bengaluru was sealed by the food safety department after finding unhygienic food handling and storage conditions, improper labelling and misbranding.

Zepto said in a statement that it had cooperated with officials and was taking steps to address their observations, the Hindustan Times reported, adding that it remained committed to food safety and hygiene standards.

In Mumbai, authorities suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after finding a large-scale cockroach infestation, improperly stored food and expired or tampered products.

Food was also found on rusted racks, while cold-storage areas lacked adequate cleanliness.

The facility has been barred from selling or distributing food or conducting any food business during the license suspension, authorities said.

Skip next section Air India pilot tests positive in drug test

Air India pilot tests positive in drug test

The captain of an Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi that suddenly lost altitude last week tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.

The Airbus A320neo, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew, lost about 300 feet of over Odisha before landing safely in Delhi.

The plane stabilized and landed safely. India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has classified the incident as serious.

The incident had left 13 passengers and four crew members injured, and led to India's aviation ministry summoning Air India CEO Campbell Wilson on Tuesday.

Skip next section Emergency at Chennai airport after IndiGo plane suffers engine failure

Emergency at Chennai airport after IndiGo plane suffers engine failure

Late on Tuesday night, Chennai airport declared a full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, media reports said.

This came only a few hours after reports emerged that the captain of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week, injuring crew and passengers, tested positive in a drug test, further plunging India's aviation into turmoil.

On Tuesday, the pilot of an IndiGo plane, flying from Kolkata to Chennai with 224 people on board, noticed that the left engine had failed while the plane prepared to land, reports said Airports Authority of India (AAI) officials.

Airport authorities activated emergency response measures, which remained in place till the plane landed safely. The declaration of full emergency was withdrawn soon after.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

The turbulence in Indian aviation continues, as Chennai airport declared a full emergency on Tuesday after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure. This comes on the heels of reports that the captain of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week, injuring crew and passengers, has tested positive in a drug test. 

Meanwhile, quick-commerce firms Zepto and Blinkit are under the scanner over "serious food safety and hygiene violations." Your deliveries may still arrive within minutes, but in what condition? That's the question.

For all this and more, stay tuned to our blog.

entries.title: Pakistan says 3 nationals killed in Houthi Red Sea attack
entries.summary: Pakistan's foreign minister has said Islamabad "strongly condemns" Houthi attacks on commercial vessels while offering condolences to the families of the dead.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan says 3 nationals killed in Houthi Red Sea attack

August 12, 2026

Pakistan's foreign minister has said Islamabad "strongly condemns" Houthi attacks on commercial vessels while offering condolences to the families of the dead.

At least three Pakistani nations were killed in an "incident involving an attack on a commercial vessel in the Red Sea," Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Wednesday. 

Another Pakistani national had sustained injuries.

"Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel. Such attacks endanger innocent lives, constitute a violation of international law, and pose a serious threat to freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea," the minister said in a post on X. 

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry was in contact with Saudi Arabia and Yemen to ascertain further details of the incident, Dar said. Meanwhile, the Pakistani Embassy in Riyadh was coordinating the retrieval and repatriation of the mortal remains of their deceased nationals.

Vessels under attack amid Middle East conflict

On Tuesday, the US and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels reported separate attacks on shipping as peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran seemingly stagnated once again.

At the southern end of the Red Sea, a suspected Houthi attack on a small cargo vessel killed four crew members, Yemen's Transport Ministry said. It was not immediately clear is this was the same vessel Dar was referring to.

Commercial shipping and seafarers passing through the Middle East have increasingly come under attack by both the US and Iran since the conflict began earlier this year. 

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Australia approves new rules benefiting gig delivery workers
entries.summary: Delivery drivers in Australia are to be guaranteed "world-leading" higher pay and insurance cover on the job. The move could be a model for other countries.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

Delivery drivers in Australia are to be guaranteed "world-leading" higher pay and insurance cover on the job. The move could be a model for other countries.

Food and grocery delivery workers in Australia will be paid at least A$31.30 (€19.15, $22.11) an hour and be given accident insurance on the job under new rules approved by Australia's industrial relations tribunal.

The hourly rate, set out in an order issued by the Fair Work Commission (FWC) on Tuesday, is above Australia's minimum wage of A$26.44.

The FWC's order, which could serve as a precedent for other countries, has been hailed by the Transport Workers Union (TWU) as "a landmark moment for the Australian gig economy." The union called the new rules a "world-leading set of standards."

What rights and protects did the FWC give gig delivery drivers?

The minimum hourly rate will be paid for "engaged" time, i.e. the time between taking on a delivery job and completing the commission.

The order, which takes effect on August 17, also requires companies to provide a "reasonable minimum level of cover" ​for personal accident insurance on the job, without specifying exactly how much.

The workers will, however, still be responsible for maintaining ⁠third-party ⁠insurance for the vehicles used for deliveries.

Unions and workers in Australia ​have long sought ⁠reforms benefiting gig workers.

They have previously not been covered by many of the protections given to other employees, being classified as "independent contractors."

The new rules are expected to affect some 250,000 workers.

UN moves to protect gig workers

The FWC's order comes after the United Nations' International Labour Organization (ILO) in June adopted a new global treaty for decent working conditions in the gig economy.

The standards laid down in the treaty, the first global treaty of its kind, still need ratification by governments.

In Australia, the parliament passed legislation in 2023 and 2024 under the center-left Labor government that granted gig workers more negotiating rights over minimum pay and working conditions.

Those laws gave the FWC the power to set rules for pay and insurance.

Edited by: Rob Turner
